stamp: EXPLORATORY. The stance κ gate is not passed.

intro.goal: This project asks how people at Bay Area public meetings feel about housing density and transit. Each statement was scored from -2, strongly opposed, to +2, strongly supportive, toward the proposal being discussed. A second pass recorded whether that proposal would add or restrict housing or transit. Each was scored three times and the median calculated. This is an exploratory analysis used to better understand the data and inspire future planned analysis.
intro.scope: Corpus: 709 meetings of 33 Bay Area bodies, 2,332 hours of video, and 15,961 scored statements, a statement being one speaker turn.

spend.text: Total spend to date $156: GPU transcription $18, stance coding $68, topic classifier $60, proposal direction $10

stance.title: Stance: the role gap
stance.stamp: EXPLORATORY. The stance κ gate is not passed.
stance.lede: The dais is where the elected officials or board members sit and run the meeting. Hostility is scored from 0 to 4 for each statement. The scale counts speech aimed at people rather than strength of disagreement. A score of 2 or higher counts as hostile.
headline: 4.9 % of public statements were coded hostile, against 0.3 % of dais statements.
74 of 100 dais statements with a stance score were coded exactly neutral, against 22 of 100 public statements.

role_pred.title: Telling officials from the public, without reading the transcript
role_pred.text: A second model is given 35 coded measures of what each speaker said, and none of the transcript. Its task is to pick the member of the public out of one public and one dais speaker. It picks correctly 8 times out of 10, against 5 times out of 10 for chance. What separates the two is how strong an opinion a statement carries, not which side it is on.
role_pred.detail: The features are stance, hostility, the twelve frames, sub-topic and length, and two of them do nearly all the work: dropping absolute stance costs 0.14 of AUC and dropping length 0.04, with nothing else over 0.02. Signed stance on its own is at chance: 0.44 by cluster, against 0.50 for a coin. So the model is not learning who is a NIMBY, it is learning who holds a position at all. Two caveats. Calibration does not travel: the ranking holds between bodies but the probabilities do not, at a slope of 0.63 out of body, so this is a measurement of how separable the two roles are and not a classifier anyone should point at a new city. And the target here is the diarization-cue role. Fitted against the audited role the same model reaches 0.86, but that number is circular. The audit is itself built from what a speaker says about who they are, so the model is partly predicting its own input.
role_pred.holdout: leave-one-body-out (every meeting of a body held out together)
role_pred.audited_note: The audited role is itself derived from what the speaker says about who they are, so a content model predicting it is partly predicting its own input. These AUCs are not comparable to the cue-role ones.

model_free.note: Model-free contrast, 2,000 episode-cluster bootstrap reps, under the reported role (corrected 2026-10-18 after role audit). Shares are among turns with a numeric stance. Turns with no stance to code are 19.5 % of public turns and 47.1 % of dais turns. Every tail gap is larger than under the older cue-phrase role, on both outcomes and in every family.
model_free.cue_note: The same contrast under the old diarization-cue role, kept as a sensitivity. It reproduces what this panel published before 2026-10-18 exactly, so the difference is the role column and nothing else.

caveats.name: The κ ≥ 0.6 hand-coding gate is not passed
caveats.text: No human has coded any of these turns. The 0.98 replicate κ is the instrument agreeing with itself (noise floor ≈ 2 %); the one cross-instrument check on record is κ 0.63 against a second codebook, same side 88 % of the time. Nothing here is a confirmatory result.

caveats.name: There is no staff role
caveats.text: Roles are dais / public / unknown. Staff reports are counted as dais, which moves the dais toward neutral. 472 unknown-role turns are outside the frame, and the computed role instrument (35 classifier episodes) is a separate, wider facet rather than more data.

caveats.name: The reported role is an audit, not a gold label
caveats.text: Added 2026-10-18. The public/dais split here is role_audit (rule ra-1), which prefers the codebook's SELF_ID over the diarization-cue role. SELF_ID is model output and no human has checked it. 7,119 of 15,961 turns (45%) say nothing about who the speaker is and keep the cue role, so the audited public bucket is still contaminated at an unknown rate. The measured error is a lower bound on the informative subset only. And the audit is a re-partition in both directions, not a cleanup: it admits cue-dais clusters as well as removing cue-public ones, and the public base with a stance *rises* from 475 to 525 clusters. Differences from the _cue numbers are not 'contamination removed'.

nimby.title: YIMBY / NIMBY
nimby.stamp: EXPLORATORY. The stance κ gate is not passed.
nimby.lede: Each statement is scored from -2 to +2 for how far it supports more housing or transit, with the sign flipped on proposals that would restrict either. A speaker is YIMBY when their statements average +0.5 or higher, NIMBY at -0.5 or lower, and neutral between. A speaker here is one voice at one meeting.
nimby.corrected: corrected 2026-10-18 after role audit; frame grown 2026-10-19 (S2)
headline: Of 525 public speakers, 44.0 % were YIMBY, 43.8 % NIMBY and 12.2 % neutral.
Petaluma, on the transcript route, had significantly more YIMBY than NIMBY public speakers (58 against 29 of 100). In the other 15 groups the difference was not significant.

role_side.title: Who takes a side
role_side.headline: Public speakers took a side on 81.4 % of the statements that carried a stance, against 32.3 % of dais statements. Public statements that took a side opposed more housing or transit significantly more often than dais ones: 52.0 % against 37.2 %.
role_side.model_line: A statement took a side when its corrected stance score was 0.5 or more away from neutral. The scale runs from -2 for opposing more housing or transit to +2 for supporting more of it.

steps.name: Took a side at all
steps.text: 9.19× the odds of taking a side, for a public statement against a dais one (likely range 6.93 to 12.32).

steps.name: Which side, given a side
steps.text: 1.60× the odds of opposing more housing or transit rather than supporting it, for a public statement against a dais one (likely range 1.15 to 2.22).

role_side.why: Behind the two steps: 81.4 % of public turns take a side rather than scoring inside the neutral band, against 32.3 % of dais turns; of the turns that do take one, 52.0 % of public turns come out against more housing or transit against 37.2 % of dais ones. The two steps are separate fits on their own rows and do not multiply together. Almost all the dependence in this corpus is inside meetings rather than between bodies: on the second step the spread between stretches of meeting is 0.96 and between meetings 0.81 on the log-odds scale, while the spread between bodies is 0.00 once meeting is in the model. Which is why the model groups turns by meeting and not by city. Renter share does not move either step: its interval covers zero on both, and so does its interaction with role. Staff speakers are dropped from these rows altogether, because they read reports rather than take positions, and a council member chairing an item is doing something other than taking one too, which is most of what the first step is measuring.

table.what: Took a side at all, of every turn with a stance
Against more housing or transit rather than for it, of the turns that took a side

role_side.table_note: Odds ratios are for a public turn against a dais one, with renter share, its interaction with role and the locate route also in the model, and with a baseline per body, per meeting and per stretch of meeting. Each likely range is a 95 % interval taken from the likelihood rather than from a standard error, which is why it is not symmetric around the estimate.
role_side.limits: The unit here is a scored turn, not a person, and both the stance score and the public/dais label are model output that no human has checked. The role label comes from what a speaker says about who they are. The first step is largely a measure of speech act rather than opinion: chairing, moving and reading a report are all neutral by construction, and they are things only the dais does. The second step's interval is slightly wider than the data require, because the optimiser stops just short of the likelihood's peak and the interval was taken at a loosened tolerance. And the permutation test once quoted for this gap has been withdrawn; the evidence here is this model and nothing else.

speakers.title: Officials were significantly more likely than public speakers to be YIMBY rather than NIMBY (70 vs 50 of 100 speakers who took a side).
speakers.text: Most officials took no side: 69 of 100, against 12 of 100 public speakers. Among those who took a side, 20 more officials than public speakers out of every 100 were YIMBY (likely range 10 to 29). An official had 2.22 times a public speaker's odds of being YIMBY rather than NIMBY (likely range 1.66 to 2.98). Both ranges are 95 % intervals.
speakers.methods_title: Officials were YIMBY rather than NIMBY more often than public speakers, 2.22 times the odds
methods: Unit and counts. The unit is one voice at one stretch of meeting, labelled as the YIMBY and NIMBY panel labels it. That means the audited role, the looser direction rule, and housing and transit proposals both counted. A speaker is YIMBY at a mean corrected stance of +0.5 or higher and NIMBY at -0.5 or lower. Officials here are every speaker the role audit placed on the dais, which includes staff reports. Of 1,497 officials with a stance, 324 were YIMBY, 139 NIMBY and 1,034 neutral. Of 525 public speakers, 231 were YIMBY, 230 NIMBY and 64 neutral.

The test. A mixed-effects logistic regression models YIMBY rather than NIMBY on role, for the speakers who took a side: 463 officials and 461 public speakers. The locate route is a fixed term and each body has its own baseline. It was fitted with lme4 (glmer, bobyqa) in R, with a 95 % profile-likelihood interval. Officials had 2.22 times the odds (likely range 1.66 to 2.98, Wald p below 0.000001, likelihood-ratio p below 0.000001). The body baseline has a standard deviation of 0.46 on the log-odds scale. A route baseline in place of the fixed term came out at zero variance. The plain logistic regression, with no body baseline, gives 2.28 times the odds (1.74 to 3.01). Among speakers who took a side, the YIMBY share differs by 19.9 of 100, with a likely range of 9.8 to 29.1. That range comes from 2,000 bootstrap draws that resample stretches of meeting inside each body and route, as the panel's own ranges do.

What it rests on. 69 of 100 officials took no side, so the test compares the 31 of 100 who did. Their 463 labels come from 24 bodies, but 50 of 100 come from three: Santa Clara, Petaluma and Napa. Without Santa Clara, the largest, the odds ratio is 2.27 (likely range 1.65 to 3.15). With a separate baseline per meeting added it is 2.15 (1.55 to 3.00). The difference points the same way inside 5 of the 5 routes. Its range excludes zero on its own only on the captions and full recording routes. Code: analysis/role_yimby_nimby_test.py and analysis/r/role_yimby_nimby.R, outputs in output/role_yimby_nimby_fullset/. Spend on 2026-10-24: $0, since the test reuses the existing scores and ran on this project's own computer.

Before and after the move to the full statement set. On the 2026-10-18 frame the same code gave 2.14 times the odds (likely range 1.48 to 3.10) on 525 speakers who took a side. Of those, 72.7 of 100 officials and 54.2 of 100 public speakers were YIMBY. On the full statement set it gives 2.22 times the odds (1.66 to 2.98) on 924, with 70.0 and 50.1 of 100. The conclusion is the same. Outputs of the first run: output/role_yimby_nimby/.

caveats.name: How a speaker gets a label, and what the label is not
caveats.text: A speaker is YIMBY at a mean corrected stance of ≥ +0.5, NIMBY at ≤ −0.5, neutral between. Housing and transit proposals both count, since the corrected score reads as support for more of either. Each route gets its own table and figure and nothing is pooled, because routes that read the same body can disagree.

caveats.name: What the correction did, and whether San Leandro drives the result
caveats.text: A separate pass read each stretch of discussion three times and recorded whether its proposal would add or restrict housing or transit; the score was flipped on the restricting ones, and rent rules, open public comment and stretches the three reads disagreed on were left out. 474 of 1212 stretches survive that, 55 of them with the sign flipped. Dropping San Leandro, the body whose rent-stabilisation items the old reading inverted, moves the split from 44.0 / 43.8 / 12.2 to 44.1 / 44.1 / 11.8.

caveats.name: Most speaker labels rest on one scored statement
caveats.text: 83.8 % of labels rest on exactly one scored statement, and a speaker averages 1.21 of them. A speaker here is one voice inside one meeting, as separated by the diarizer: one person split in two counts twice, and two people merged count once.

Only 1 of the 16 groups differed significantly: Petaluma, on the transcript route

fullset_note.title: The YIMBY and NIMBY view moved onto the full statement set on 2026-10-24, and its conclusions held
paragraphs: On 2026-10-24, at the owner's request, the published YIMBY and NIMBY view moved from the frame of 2026-10-18 to the full statement set. The old frame held 9,358 statements. It left out 3,680 statements scored on 2026-10-19 and 20 and all 2,923 statements on the full recording route. The full set holds every scored statement, 15,961 in all. By route: 7,161 on the captions route, 2,923 on the full recording route, 2,572 on the own audio route, 2,153 on the agenda index route and 1,152 on the transcript route. After the direction pass's exclusions, 6,657 of them carry a speaker label, against 4,235 before.

A route is which transcript source a meeting came from. The captions route uses YouTube captions. The transcript route uses a city's own transcript. The agenda index route cuts the meeting at the agenda item's time stamp. The own audio route is audio this project transcribed itself. The full recording route transcribed the whole meeting from its audio and checked every 2-minute window for the topic, with no keyword screen. Its statements come from housing stretches only. Routes are never pooled.

Before and after. Public speakers with a stance: 274 before, 525 after. Of every 100, YIMBY 46.7 and NIMBY 39.4 before, YIMBY 44.0 and NIMBY 43.8 after. Body and route groups with at least 10 public speakers: 8 before, 16 after. Groups with a significant difference: 1 before (Petaluma on the transcript route) and 1 after (Petaluma on the transcript route). The star rule, the direction rule and the seed did not change. The role test and the renter regression were fit again on the full set. Their entries in section 5 give both results.

Code: analysis/build_full_frame.py writes the frame, output/stance_s1/full_frame_2026-10-24.csv. analysis/stance_s1_role_audit_view.py runs on it and writes output/stance_s1/nimby_view_fullset/. The 2026-10-18 frame, output/stance_s1/s1_frame.csv, and its outputs are kept. analysis/fullset_before_after.py prints the full table. plan/DECISIONS.md records it as a dated note under decision 20. Spend on 2026-10-24: $0.

renter.title: Renter share
renter.stamp: EXPLORATORY. The stance κ gate is not passed.
renter.lede: Renter share is the renter-occupied share of a body's occupied housing units, from the American Community Survey.
headline: Renter share had no significant link to what was said at meetings.

A staff member in a California county government suggested renter share as a main predictor, as a lead for future work. Each body's share of public statements opposing more housing or transit was regressed on renter share, median household income and population density. No predictor was significant in the 28 body-and-route groups, with every likely range a 95 % interval. Every 10 more renter-occupied homes out of 100 went with 1.14 times the odds of an opposing statement (likely range 0.71 to 1.88). Renter share also had no significant link to YIMBY share or to meeting time on housing density and transit.

refit.title: Renter share had no significant link to what was said at meetings.
refit.page_text: A staff member in a California county government suggested renter share as a main predictor, as a lead for future work. Each body's share of public statements opposing more housing or transit was regressed on renter share, median household income and population density. No predictor was significant in the 28 body-and-route groups, with every likely range a 95 % interval. Every 10 more renter-occupied homes out of 100 went with 1.14 times the odds of an opposing statement (likely range 0.71 to 1.88). Renter share also had no significant link to YIMBY share or to meeting time on housing density and transit.
refit.methods_title: Renter share still had no significant link to NIMBY share after the direction correction
methods: The renter-share regression of 2026-10-18 was fit again on 2026-10-24 on the corrected scores of the full statement set. It used the same code, priors, sampler settings and seed (analysis/renter_share7_direction_models.py, calling the fitting functions of analysis/renter_share_models.py). A body on one route enters with 5 or more public statements carrying a stance. The outcome is how many of those statements opposed more housing or transit, a corrected stance of -0.5 or lower. It is a binomial count with a route term and an overdispersion term per group. Renter share, log median household income and log population density enter standardised, each with a Normal(0, 1) prior. Coefficients below are log-odds per standard deviation with 95 % posterior intervals.

Before and after. Published: 20 groups, 18 bodies, 500 statements. Renter share -0.13 (-0.68 to +0.42), income +0.17 (-0.41 to +0.72), density -0.07 (-0.66 to +0.57). Corrected, on the 2026-10-18 frame: 17 groups, 14 bodies, 337 statements. Renter share -0.07 (-0.66 to +0.54), income -0.04 (-0.66 to +0.59), density -0.02 (-0.61 to +0.60). Corrected, on the full statement set: 28 groups, 21 bodies, 649 statements. Renter share +0.11 (-0.30 to +0.56), with a 0.71 posterior probability above zero. Income -0.13 (-0.52 to +0.26), density -0.05 (-0.46 to +0.35). Largest R-hat 1.001, 0 divergent transitions, 28 of 28 groups inside the 90 % posterior predictive band. Without the correction, the same model on today's statements gives renter share -0.09 (-0.43 to +0.26) on 37 groups. So the change is partly the correction and partly the statements added since 2026-10-18.

The other fits. YIMBY share on renter share alone: renter share -0.12 (-0.40 to +0.15), 28 groups. YIMBY share with the two covariates: renter share -0.12 (-0.44 to +0.19), 28 groups. Minutes on housing density and transit per meeting hour, complete-coverage groups: renter share +0.93 (-0.24 to +1.94), 12 groups. The same with partial-coverage groups added and flagged: renter share -0.10 (-0.52 to +0.31), 78 groups. Minutes on housing density alone, all groups: renter share -0.23 (-0.60 to +0.12), 39 groups. The meeting-time fits read the located topic minutes, which the correction does not touch; they moved because the coverage test was fixed on 2026-10-20. Sampling was rough in 3 fits, so their intervals are approximate. YIMBY share with the two covariates: R-hat 1.035, 0 divergent transitions. Minutes on housing density and transit per meeting hour, complete-coverage groups: R-hat 1.005, 54 divergent transitions. Minutes on housing density alone, all groups: R-hat 1.017, 0 divergent transitions. Outputs: output/renter_share_fullset_direction_loose/, with the published fit kept in output/renter_share/models/ and the 2026-10-18-frame re-fit in output/renter_share_direction_loose/. Spend on 2026-10-24: $0, since the re-fit ran on this project's own computer.

caveats.name: How little this could have detected: n is the finding
caveats.text: “No relationship” here means “no relationship this design could see”. Each correlation rests on 15 to 20 bodies with a median of 18 scored public turns each, which could only have detected an effect several times larger than any plausible one. The 90 % interval on the NIMBY slope runs from a large negative effect to a moderate positive one, and so does the interval on every other outcome tested. Read the null as a statement about the sample size, not about renter share. And a sharp result here would still be a statement about cities rather than about the people who show up to speak at their meetings: the covariate is a body's whole renter share, not anything known about a speaker.

caveats.name: The rate correlations should not be quoted at all yet
caveats.text: Both rate rows are computed on the as-published 7-body complete-coverage set. The coverage test has since been fixed and the complete set is 5 bodies, so on a rerun today those rows fall to n = 3 on the classifier route. The local_asr and agenda_index rate figures drop below the 3-body floor entirely and have been moved to output/renter_share/_stale_pre_coverage_fix/.

caveats.name: Transit boards are marked hollow, and a councils-only panel is drawn beside each figure
caveats.text: A transit board's topic time mostly measures what it exists to do, so every figure draws the boards with hollow markers and carries a councils-only panel wherever one can be drawn above the 3-body floor. Read the councils-only panel first.

rates.title: Topic time per meeting-hour
rates.stamp: Rates are a measurement, not a model estimate. Each likely range is a 95 % episode bootstrap.
headline: The two transit boards gave housing density and transit the most meeting time: BART 29.14 and VTA 27.00 minutes of each meeting-hour.
Napa County gave them 1.78 to 2.48 minutes, depending on which route read the meeting.

caveats.name: Most of these rates are floors
caveats.text: Only bart, napa, samtrans, sausalito, vta have had every meeting read. Fremont, Hayward, Petaluma, Richmond, San Leandro and Santa Clara are part-read, so their rates are floors. samtrans, sausalito publish no video length, so they get no rate at all.

caveats.name: Which route read a body moves its rate as much as the body does
caveats.text: Hayward measures 0.65 min/h on one route, 1.73 on another and 4.17 on a third. BART is at 29.1 min/h and VTA at 27.0, and Napa at 1.8 to 2.2 on all three of its routes. So route is a column in every table here and nothing is pooled.

caveats.name: Density does not outweigh transit everywhere
caveats.text: An earlier draft said it did. Hayward on the classifier route is 0.1 density against 0.4 transit, and Petaluma's Swagit route 7.2 against 8.2.
